Pacific sand lance (Ammodytes hexapterus) exhibits a life history closely tied to the cold, productive waters of the North Pacific. During the spawning season, which typically occurs in late autumn to early winter, females deposit adhesive, demersal eggs on coarse sandy substrates in intertidal and shallow subtidal zones. At the prevailing bottom temperatures of 3.4 °C [T = 3.4 °C], the incubation period is approximately 19 days [ab = approximately 19 days], after which the prolarvae emerge. These newly hatched yolk-sac larvae are extremely small, possessing an estimated wet weight of only 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams], a mass derived from the typical egg diameter of 0.9 millimeters observed in congeneric species. This diminutive size at birth reflects the straightforward life-history strategy of a species that invests in numerous small eggs rather than provisioning large yolk reserves for a prolonged endotrophic phase. The larvae are initially lecithotrophic, relying entirely on endogenous yolk for the first few days post-hatching.

Following the depletion of yolk reserves, the larvae of Pacific sand lance undergo the exotrophic transition, at which point they begin feeding on small copepod nauplii and other microzooplankton. This early larval period is a critical bottleneck for recruitment, as mortality rates are exceptionally high during the first weeks of exogenous feeding. Growth during the pelagic larval phase is rapid, driven by the abundant spring phytoplankton bloom that sustains their zooplankton prey. The pelagic juvenile stage eventually gives way to a metamorphic event marked by the development of the distinctive pointed snout and the elongated, silver-sided body plan characteristic of the species. As individuals approach the onset of sexual maturation, they have typically attained a standard length of 11 centimeters [Lp = 11 centimeters]. This measurement serves as a key indicator that an individual is entering the transition toward reproductive competence. Most fish in the population reach this length after their first full year of growth, though local variation in thermal regimes can influence this trajectory.

The onset of puberty in Pacific sand lance is closely linked to both body size and seasonal cues, with individuals generally achieving a standard length of 11 centimeters [Lp = 11 centimeters] before gonadal development commences. By the time this length is reached, the average wet weight of a fish at puberty is approximately 4.9 grams [Wwp = approximately 4.9 grams], a substantial increase from the larval stage. This reproductive mass represents the culmination of a period of intensive somatic growth, during which energy is primarily directed toward increasing body length and accumulating lipid reserves in the visceral cavity. These reserves are critical for fuelling the metabolic demands of the overwintering period and subsequent gamete production in the following spring. Males and females show little dimorphism in size-at-maturity, and first spawning for both sexes typically occurs at the same body length and weight threshold. The transition from a purely somatic growth phase to one incorporating reproductive investment is a key life-history event, determining a fish’s lifetime fitness and its contribution to the next generation.

The maximum standard length attained by Pacific sand lance in most populations across its range is approximately 30 centimeters [Li = approximately 30 centimeters]. Individuals that achieve this ultimate size are relatively rare, as growth slows considerably after the onset of maturity and is strongly modulated by prey availability and environmental conditions. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for a fish of this length is roughly 115.6 grams [Wwi = roughly 115.6 grams], representing the upper boundary of the species' size range. These large adults are typically the most fecund members of the population, producing a greater number of eggs per spawning event than younger or smaller conspecifics. The capacity to reach such a size is linked to the species’ annual growth cycle, which involves intensive feeding during the spring and summer months followed by a period of inactivity and fasting while buried in the sand during the winter. This behavioral adaptation to seasonal food limitation has a direct impact on the maximum body size achievable in a given environment.

The lifespan of Pacific sand lance is relatively constrained compared to many other temperate marine fishes, with most individuals living no more than 11 years [am = 11 years] under the cold-water conditions of 3.4 °C [T = 3.4 °C] that characterize their habitat. This maximum age is typically reached only by a small fraction of the population, given the intense predation pressure from piscivorous fish, seabirds, and marine mammals throughout their lives. The species follows an iteroparous reproductive strategy, spawning multiple times over its adult lifespan once the pubertal size and weight thresholds have been crossed. Annual adult survival is moderate, and the age structure of a typical spawning aggregation reveals that the majority of breeding individuals are between two and five years old. The relatively short lifespan, combined with the small body size at puberty and the extremely low wet weight at birth (0.00038 grams) [Wwb = 0.00038 grams], underscores a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproduction and high fecundity over extended somatic growth and longevity in a highly variable and predator-rich ecosystem.
